View of Mineros' Nechi Alluvial operation in Colombia. Credit: Mineros.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 13, 2026
Mineros (TSX: MSA; US-OTC: MNSAF) bought $137.3 million (C$195.7 million) of bullion in the third quarter and expanded its borrowing against physical gold, drawing an analyst warning that its treasury strategy is adding risk despite strong mining profits.
The purchases pushed reported quarterly operating cash flow below zero, Mineros said Wednesday . Mineros ended September with $54 million in cash and $127.7 million in borrowings, then added gold-backed financing agreements that require additional cash collateral if prices fall, according to its quarterly filings.
“We continue to view the treasury strategy negatively and now add margin call exposure to the risks,” Red Cloud mining analyst Alina Islam said Friday in a note. Mineros’ treasury strategy “is taking up a growing share of the balance sheet and adding leverage.”
Increased exposure
The strategy increases Mineros’ exposure to the metal beyond the gold it produces in Colombia and Nicaragua. Higher bullion prices could benefit its holdings, but a decline could create calls for cash at the same time weaker prices reduce mining revenue.
The company’s explanation is that retaining exposure to gold aligns its treasury with investors who buy the shares for exposure to the sector. Management considers the holdings part of its capital-management policy, CEO Daniel Henao said.
“This position reflects our view that gold remains an effective long-term store of value in the current macroeconomic environment,” Henao said in the results release.
Borrowing against bullion
Mineros already had 15,601 oz. of gold tied to repurchase agreements at Sept. 30. Its Swiss subsidiary posted 20,000 oz. of gold on Oct. 16 for net proceeds of $73.2 million after an $8.7-million cash collateral deposit, followed by 8,981 oz. on Oct. 29 for $32 million.
Repurchase obligations fall due in October 2027 and February 2027, respectively. Mineros guarantees the obligations and retains the exposure to changes in gold prices.
Islam calculated that about 88% of the company’s physical gold was pledged under the agreements. That estimate combines September’s pledged gold with the October transactions and assumes no intervening changes in holdings or earlier agreements.
Borrowings at the September quarter-end were more than eight times their level at the end of 2025, before the October transactions.
Forward contract
The gold exposure also included a forward contract to buy 18,650 oz. at $4,740 per oz. As of Sept. 30, Mineros recorded a $10.5-million liability on that contract and had posted $12.5 million in cash margin. It also recognized an $11.9-million non-cash write-down on allocated bullion.
The financing comes as shareholders prepare to vote on a special dividend of 20¢ a share, totalling about $58 million, at a Nov. 24 meeting. The proposal was announced Oct. 23, between the two gold-backed financing transactions.
If approved, the payment would be made Dec. 4 to shareholders of record Dec. 1, in addition to the ordinary dividend. Mineros expects to fund it from cash on hand and operating cash flow.
As of Sept. 30, the company also reported $145.4 million of unpledged precious metals in its net cash calculation, which put net cash at $71.7 million after borrowings. That company-defined measure treats available precious metals as cash equivalents for this calculation.
Strong quarter
The mining business delivered quarterly adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $140 million, 55% more than a year earlier, the company reported. Net income was $89.5 million, or 30¢ a share, compared with 18¢ a year earlier. The realized gold price averaged $4,301 per ounce.
Reported operating cash flow was negative $21.6 million after bullion purchases. Before those purchases, the company’s operating cash flow before strategic gold purchases was positive $115.7 million.
Quarterly gold production rose 13% to 62,253 ounces. Mineros’ full-year forecast stands at 235,000 to 245,000 oz., following an increase announced in October. Its Hemco plant expansion in Nicaragua is due for completion by year-end.
The stronger earnings, index inclusion, share buybacks and proposed dividend could all support the stock in the near term, Islam said.
Mineros shares dropped 3.4% to C$8.53 in Toronto Friday afternoon, valuing the company at about C$2.5 billion. That cut their gain since the start of the year to about 56%.
“Gold that cannot be sold or repledged, and that may require margin calls in a falling market, is better viewed as collateral, not liquidity,” Islam said.

Businesses will pay more next year to ship packages through the U.S. Postal Service, which is pushing through another round of pricing and fee adjustments.
The Postal Service notified the Postal Regulatory Commission on Thursday about its intent to raise domestic and international shipping rates and surcharges, effective Jan. 17.
The agency wants to pass on additional shipping expenses to businesses and households because higher diesel costs and declining mail volume are putting sustained pressure on postal finances. Postmaster General David Steiner has made revenue growth a key priority since taking the helm 18 months ago.
The most impactful increase is a new, permanent fuel surcharge pegged at 11% of the total shipping bill. The fuel surcharge, which is aimed at recovering heavy diesel fuel expenditures for its truck and delivery fleet after the Iran war caused prices to shoot up, is three points higher than originally proposed less than three weeks ago and the temporary transportation fee implemented in April , which is set to expire on Jan. 17.
The Postal Service, which reduced its operating loss last year to $2.4 billion , last month disclosed plans to implement an 8% fuel surcharge. It will be the first-ever permanent fuel surcharge for the national post, as it adopts a practice common among private courier fleets.
The agency said the surcharge, which will not apply to international products at this time, will be reevaluated in July based on fuel prices in the first half of 2027.
The fuel surcharge is an extra hit for shippers, but is significantly less than the 28% to 30% fuel surcharges being collected by FedEx and UPS, and only applies to base postage.
The adjustments would raise domestic shipping service prices 5.9% on average for Priority Mail service, Priority Mail Express, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select products, matching the 5.9% general rate increases from FedEx and United Parcel Service for next year.
The USPS will also increase prices on some competitive special services and introduce new fees commonly charged by private sector competitors. Shippers, for example, will pay more than 20% on shortpaid postage because of inaccurate weight or volume calculations, for example. Non-compliant shipping labels will incur a $5 fee per parcel. Other fees cover address enhancement services, premium forwarding, and ancillary services.
Drilling into specific product changes shows that short zones bear the brunt of the price increase. Priority Mail packages up to five pounds will cost 7% more, with an 11.6% increase for short-to-mid range regional distances and 4.4% for longer distances. Ground Advantage, the most economical product, is slated to go up 6.9% for packages under one pound, on top of July’s elimination of ounce pricing for commercial rates. One pound boxes destined for short-and-intermediate zones get an 11.9% increase, on average.
Parcel Select packages are priced 5.5% to 6% higher, depending on weight.
Why It Matters: Parcel shippers are feeling the impact of add-on fees. Hikes in the fuel surcharge and new fees for heavier packages and premium services helped push up ground and express parcel costs by 5.2% and 5.9% year over year for ground and express parcels, respectively, during the third quarter.
International changes
In addition to increasing domestic competitive rates, the Postal Service is adjusting international mail and shipping rates as well as the country rate group structure and group assignments. The adjustments will raise prices by an average of 7.9% for regular and express international products.
The Postal Service said it is also introducing a new optional Outbound Proof of Delivery service for Priority Mail International and expanding USPS Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) service to include International Priority Airmail. The change in the DDP service will allow outbound customers to pay the duties while mailing or at a later time.
“The USPS governors believe these new rates will keep the Postal Service competitive while providing the agency with much needed revenue as it continues to struggle with financial issues,” the agency said in a news release.

Robert Friedland at the Future Minerals Forum in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. (Image provided by FMF.)
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie November 13, 2026
Ivanhoe Atlantic has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Pakistan’s Mari Minerals, a subsidiary of Mari Energies (PSX: MARI), to pursue mineral exploration opportunities in Balochistan province, marking the United States-based strategic metals company’s entry into South Asia.
Billionaire Robert Friedland announced the agreement Thursday, on the sidelines of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum. Friedland is the founder and chairman of I-Pulse Inc., a United States-based company that holds a majority stake in Ivanhoe Atlantic.
Ivanhoe Atlantic is developing the Kon Kweni iron ore project in Guinea, its main asset. It is a separate company from Toronto-listed Ivanhoe Mines (TSX: IVN; US-OTC: IVPAF).
Venture operator
Under the proposed joint venture, Ivanhoe Atlantic would serve as operator and conduct early-stage exploration across a package of mineral licences in Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province. The companies plan to combine Ivanhoe’s technical and financing expertise with Mari Minerals’ local knowledge and operating experience.
Friedland said Ivanhoe Atlantic was beginning to establish a local office and expected to sign another agreement Friday, according to Reuters . Mari Minerals, the mining subsidiary of Mari Energies, has several copper and gold exploration projects in Pakistan.
“We’re forming equal partnerships,” Friedland told reporters when asked about the MOU’s structure and timeline. He said the company is seeking to bring international expertise to Pakistan to accelerate mineral discoveries.
Equal partnerships
While Friedland indicated that Ivanhoe Atlantic intends to pursue equal partnerships in Pakistan, he didn’t confirm whether the agreement with Mari Minerals would follow a 50-50 ownership structure.
The MOU, which is non-binding except for certain customary provisions, outlines the principal terms of the proposed joint venture, but the companies must still negotiate definitive agreements, secure corporate and regulatory approvals, establish the joint venture entity and transfer the relevant exploration licences. Financial terms and a timetable for completing the transaction haven’t been disclosed.
The move gives Ivanhoe Atlantic a foothold in a largely underexplored mineral jurisdiction as Pakistan seeks foreign capital and technical expertise to develop its copper and gold resources. Ivanhoe Atlantic said the proposed partnership also aligns with Washington’s efforts to diversify critical mineral supply chains, particularly for copper used in electricity grids, data centres, advanced manufacturing and defence. Security concerns and infrastructure challenges remain significant obstacles to attracting international investment.
Exploration potential
Friedland said the venture would draw on experience from Friedland-linked companies in Mongolia, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Saudi Arabia as it establishes a presence in Pakistan.
Pakistan’s copper and gold potential is supported by a vast mineralized geological belt extending from Turkey and Iran through Afghanistan and Pakistan into western China and Mongolia, Friedland told MINING.COM. Balochistan, which lies within the mineral-rich Tethyan Metallogenic Belt. hosts relatively few operating mines despite its extensive mineral potential.
“Pakistan is profoundly unexplored,” Friedland said in an interview Thursday, pointing to advances in geophysical surveying, remote sensing and artificial intelligence that could help identify deposits more quickly than traditional exploration methods.
Immediate priority
Ivanhoe Atlantic ‘s immediate priority is to finalize the agreements and mobilize a technically rigorous exploration program, director Bradley Doig said.
Mari Minerals managing director and CEO Faheem Haider expects the partnership to focus on unlocking the potential of the Chagai belt, drawing on Mari Energies’ decades of operating experience in Pakistan.
Successful mining development depends on local communities sharing directly in the economic benefits, including employment, education and infrastructure improvements, Friedland added.
Drawing on his experience in Africa, the executive said community participation is essential to securing long-term support for mining operations and avoiding disputes that can disrupt projects.
Mari Minerals and Mari Energies chairman Anwar Ali Hyder echoed that emphasis, saying the partnership should generate jobs, skills development, local business opportunities and infrastructure improvements.
Investment challenges
Pakistan has been courting foreign mining companies to help unlock its mineral wealth, including plans announced last year to offer concessions to U.S. investors as part of broader tariff negotiations with Washington, Reuters reported.
Ivanhoe Atlantic executive chairman J. Peter Pham said the proposed venture had received encouragement from the US government and Pakistani federal authorities, reflecting growing cooperation between the two countries on critical minerals.
The country hosts major copper and gold deposits, including Reko Diq in Balochistan, one of the world’s largest undeveloped copper-gold projects. The project is being developed through a joint venture involving Barrick Mining, Pakistan’s federal government and the Balochistan provincial government.
However, the investment push faces significant obstacles. Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX; NYSE: B) said earlier this year it would slow development and extend its review of Reko Diq until mid-2027 amid escalating security concerns in Pakistan and the Middle East, underscoring the risks facing foreign companies operating in the region.
Developing new mines will also require substantial investment in transport infrastructure, energy and skilled labour. Friedland said lessons from Ivanhoe Mines’ Kamoa-Kakula copper complex in the DRC demonstrate the importance of reliable rail and port connections to make large-scale mining competitive. Print

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.
Volkswagen EV delays persist
As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.
“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters . The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.
Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.
Volkswagen Golf EV preview (Source: Volkswagen)
Now, it’s the Audi A4 E-Tron
According to Autocar , Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.
Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.
Audi-A6-E-tron
BMW has the new i3 , and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.
Volkswagen said in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.
The company also said investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”
Audi A4 sedan (Source: Audi)
Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.
To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.
In March, VW said several test vehicles , including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.
Volkswagen ID.EVERY1 with Rivian SDV architecture during testing (Source: Volkswagen)
However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.
Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.
The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.
While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

source_document.body:
For most carriers, growth follows a familiar script: buy a truck, then buy or lease a trailer to go behind it. Repeat. The script is simple, but it ties up scarce capital in depreciating equipment over its life, or locks in a long-term contract, often before a carrier knows whether the freight to support it will last.
Matt Harb, Chief Product Officer at REPOWR, spends much of his day talking with carriers who are living that tradeoff. Speaking with The Long Haul at F3 in Chattanooga, Harb said his goal in those conversations is to understand what carriers need from the trailer on their back, though the discussion rarely stays there. “They’re feeling the heat from every different part of the industry,” he said, pointing to fuel costs, broker relationships, and the hunt for good loads as constant pressures.
REPOWR’s answer is a trailer-sharing marketplace that lets fleets access trailer capacity short-term instead of committing to long-term capex, now backed by software built for the fleets that supply the trailers.
How the marketplace works
REPOWR works with large and mid-sized fleets to reduce repositioning costs, giving small fleets short-term access to equipment. Harb said the platform carries about 3,500 trailers nationwide at any moment, including flatbeds, reefers, and dry vans, with rentals ranging from three days to 90 days. Roughly 75 fleets list equipment in a given month.
Rates are daily, with no hidden fees, and carriers pick up and return trailers with inspection forms at both ends. In many cases, Harb said, another trailer is waiting at the drop location. He acknowledged that the Airbnb comparison is not universally loved inside the company, but conceded it fits. “We’re Airbnb or Turvo for trailers,” he said.
The model also works both ways. Carriers that need repositioning or have idle trailers can list them for others to use, which Harb said can offset payments or generate extra revenue during slow stretches or while a carrier is committed to power-only work for the holidays.
The hidden price of power-only
Power-only has grown because it removes the capital commitment of owning a trailer. Harb argued that it also removes something carriers rarely price in. “They give up control mostly,” he said. Filtering a load board for power-only freight, he noted, typically leaves a fraction of the available loads. “You’re giving up lanes. You’re giving up better rates,” he said.
Control, in his view, is what carriers trade away, and it quickly becomes a flexibility problem. “Control is the biggest piece, and control really kind of boils over into flexibility,” Harb said.
To help carriers who need a trailer for a limited stretch, REPOWER recently launched short-run pricing. For most trailers on the marketplace, rentals shorter than 14 days run at nearly half the usual cost. Suppliers benefit because their equipment gets repositioned faster, which is how the company can offer the lower rate. The same logic applies to repositioning generally: Harb said a trailer owner who relies on a loadout broker may pay $500 to $600 for a move that REPOWR’s platform can handle at little or no cost.
Renting as a way to test the market
Harb said the most common mistake he sees is not about equipment type. It is about business structure: attaching long-term capital to a decision before it has been tested.
He described a 15-truck fleet that regularly rents 10 to 15 trailers a month on the platform and was preparing to buy three trucks and long-term lease reefers because shippers had promised good lanes. His advice was to rent first. The economics of buying are steep. “A trailer is not eight grand anymore. I mean, a new dry van trailer is $45,000, and a used one needs to be under 10 years old for many shippers,” Harb said.
What rental does, he said, is let carriers experiment: “It’s the flexibility to change quickly, to add quickly, to reduce quickly, and to do all that without any sunk costs.” Buying or signing a long-term lease, by contrast, means “you’ve just hitched your wagon to a depreciating asset.”
That approach also applies to adapting to shippers. Harb said he often hears from carriers whose customers change specifications, such as a move from roll-door equipment to swing-door trailers, leaving them stuck with a trailer they committed to for 12 months. Some carriers use REPOWR on both sides, listing the equipment they cannot use and renting what the shipper now wants. “You can stay agile as those shippers’ needs change,” Harb said.
Drop-and-hook without owning the trailers
Harb said he believes the vast majority of freight now moves through drop-and-hook, and he argued that some carriers assume they are locked out because they cannot meet the trailer-to-tractor ratios shippers want, commonly three-to-one or more. REPOWR changes that, because a carrier can match a trailer commitment to the length of the project. “You’re not matching a short-term commitment to a long-term commitment,” he said.
Quality, accountability and onboarding
REPOWR takes safety and security seriously. Pickup and return inspection forms categorize trailer issues, and the company scores fleet quality, which affects how listings rank and are priced. Harb said REPOWR has stopped working with suppliers whose equipment repeatedly was not there when carriers arrived.
Accountability runs both ways. Carriers’ insurance is on file, and every listing details equipment such as air-ride or spring-ride suspension and swing or roll doors. “It’s our job to hold both accountable,” Harb said.
To join, carriers need at least six months of active authority and must clear a Persona identity verification, Highway authority check, and a safety-screen phone call that Harb said filters out applicants. Signing up is free and takes about six minutes using DOT number and identity verification. Booking a trailer takes about seven minutes and requires two certificates of insurance, one naming the supplier as additionally insured. Harb said 85% of pickups happen the same day or the next day. Rentals are charged in 30-day increments, with no extensive credit check.
The supply side: automating trailer repositioning with TOP
The marketplace only works if trailers are available where carriers need them, which is the challenge REPOWR’s Trailer Optimization Platform , or TOP, is built to solve. In the interview, Harb described the logic behind the low rental rates: “We’re stopping them from having to have all this idle equipment or pay for these repositions.”
According to REPOWR, TOP is an automated capacity planning platform designed to execute trailer repositioning, not just analyze it. The company says fleets typically pay to reposition about 3% of their trailers each month, usually through phone calls, spreadsheets, and brokers at $400 or more per move. Harb puts the going rate for a loadout broker at $500 to $600, but this number increases when capacity is tight.
Here is how the platform works:
Import the network. Fleets share trailers and locations by CSV, data feed, or TMS integration.
Set targets. Locations roll up into markets, each with a target trailer range.
Balance automatically. When a market runs long, TOP lists surplus trailers on the REPOWR marketplace. Carriers reserve and move them as part of normal activity.
The result, REPOWR says, is that a repositioning move earns revenue for the trailer owner instead of costing money. For carriers renting on the platform, it also means a steadier supply of equipment in more markets.
REPOWR’s illustrative model for a 2,500-trailer fleet puts annual repositioning costs at $225,000 without TOP and $135,000 with it. Adding coordination costs and marketplace revenue, the company projects total savings of about $197,000 a year. Those are the company’s projections, not independent results. REPOWR says a 6,000-trailer fleet was onboarded in two days, and that the platform is built for fleets of 150 or more trailers.
Fleets can send 90 days of repositioning data, and REPOWR says it will return a projected savings analysis with no commitment required.
A warning on rental fraud
Harb closed with a caution for the whole industry as trailer rental scams target owner-operators. His rule is blunt. “Nobody is doing trailer rentals with Zelle or Cash App,” he said. Carriers should talk to a person, verify that the provider owns the equipment, and treat unrealistic prices as a warning sign. “I saw one that was $180 for three months of a trailer, like maybe rethink that,” he said. He added that scammers are copying branding and websites. “People are spoofing websites now.”
His message to carriers weighing their next equipment move was simple: “You don’t have to be stuck.”

By: Staff Writer November 13, 2026
Ten people have been killed in clashes between security forces and protesters in Guinea’s northeastern gold-producing region of Siguiri, the government said, as a crackdown on illegal and unregulated gold mining triggers mass expulsions and a growing humanitarian crisis in neighbouring countries.
The violence erupted Wednesday at Balato when defence and security forces attempted to enforce a Nov. 2 ban on illegal and unregulated gold mining. Protesters erected barricades on public roads before the confrontation escalated into an exchange of gunfire, Guinea’s Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralization said in a statement dated Thursday.
Five foreign nationals were among those killed, while 13 people, including civilians and security personnel, were injured, according to provisional government figures. Authorities did not disclose the nationalities of the foreign victims. Judicial authorities have been asked to establish the circumstances and determine responsibility.
The unrest highlights the growing economic and humanitarian fallout from Guinea’s efforts to curb illegal gold production in a region where artisanal mining provides livelihoods for thousands of workers and their families. Mali has warned of a humanitarian emergency, while Burkina Faso has criticized the treatment of its citizens during the expulsions.
Mass displacement
Guinea imposed the ban after authorities blamed unregulated mining operations for extensive environmental damage, including the destruction of farmland and forests and the pollution of rivers.
Security forces have arrested more than 1,300 people in the crackdown, according to a statement Thursday from prosecutors reported by Guinee7 . Trials opened this week in Conakry, and some defendants have already received prison sentences.
The enforcement campaign has driven tens of thousands of miners and their families across the border into Mali, where authorities have warned of a potential humanitarian catastrophe.
About 100,000 displaced people have arrived in Mali’s capital, Bamako, while nearly 60,000 others have gathered in the border town of Kouremale, according to figures released by Malian authorities on Nov. 7.
Ten deaths linked to the displacement crisis have been recorded in Mali, Agence France-Presse reported Friday, separate from the fatalities reported in Guinea.
Burkina Faso, meanwhile, had received and registered 45,406 returnees as of Thursday, according to its National Emergency Relief and Rehabilitation Council. Officials in Ouagadougou have complained that their nationals were subjected to inhumane treatment during the expulsions.
Security fears
The influx of displaced miners has raised concerns that armed extremist groups operating across the Sahel could exploit the growing humanitarian emergency to recruit vulnerable migrants.
“These people are vulnerable. We are looking at ways to prevent them from being approached by terrorist networks,” a Malian security ministry official told Agence France-Presse .
Guinea, the world’s largest bauxite producer, also hosts industrial gold mines, including AngloGold Ashanti ’s (NYSE: AU) Siguiri operation. The company owns 85% of the mine, while Guinea’s government holds the remaining 15%. Print

Less than two years after acquiring the assets, Lantheus is selling its CDMO unit and a New Jersey production plant to PharmaLogic.
PharmaLogic has struck a deal to buy a radiopharmaceutical contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) and production plant from Lantheus.
Lantheus acquired the CDMO and Springfield, New Jersey, production facility last year when it bought Evergreen Theragnostics for $250 million upfront. At the time, Lantheus hailed Evergreen’s radioligand therapy manufacturing infrastructure and revenue-generating CDMO as a boost for its business. Yet, 19 months after closing the deal, Lantheus has agreed to offload the CDMO and New Jersey plant.
PharmaLogic is buying the assets for an undisclosed sum to advance toward its goal of creating the first fully integrated, global CDMO specializing in radiopharmaceutical therapies. Buying the Springfield site will make PharmaLogic the first therapeutic CDMO to offer a transatlantic platform, the company said in a press release on Monday.
The CDMO established a presence in Europe last year by acquiring a majority stake in Norway’s Agilera Pharma. Employees at the Springfield facility will join Agilera, which will make lutetium Lu 177 dotatate for Lantheus.
The Springfield plant is a 14,000-square-foot manufacturing facility that Evergreen completed in 2021. The facility features seven commercial-scale production suites for manufacturing using a variety of isotopes. Evergreen designed the plant to handle beta emitters, such as the lutetium used in Novartis’ Lutathera and Pluvicto, and the alpha emitters found in multiple next-generation drug candidates.
The facility is equipped to support projects from early-stage trials through commercial manufacturing. Based 15 minutes from Newark’s international airport, the plant is positioned to quickly distribute radiopharmaceuticals beyond New Jersey.

Companies including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Eli Lilly have radiopharmaceuticals in development.
The nature of radioisotopes, which can decay in days and pose risks to people, necessitates specialized manufacturing and supply chain capabilities. Freightos founder and former CEO Zvi Schreiber has accused the company of “rigging” a shareholder vote by omitting one of his proposals from its proxy card. He said properly executed proxy forms would automatically count as votes against the proposal.
The proposal is included in Freightos’ proxy statement but cannot be supported through the company’s standard proxy voting process. Shareholders who want to vote in favor must attend the Dec. 16 annual general meeting in person at Freightos’ offices in Modi’in, Israel.
Schreiber has now written to the full board, giving it until Tuesday, Nov. 17, to issue a revised proxy card that allows shareholders to vote on all resolutions. He said he would “escalate” the matter if the company does not make the change. Schreiber did not comment on what that escalation would be.
The dispute comes ahead of Freightos’ Dec. 16 annual general meeting, where shareholders will consider three proposals submitted by Schreiber. In a proxy statement filed Nov. 4, Freightos urged shareholders to reject all three, which seek to remove Chairman Udo Lange, introduce annual elections for all directors and refocus the business on its digital freight-booking platform.
The proposals are the latest development in a dispute between Schreiber and Freightos over the company’s direction and financial performance. Schreiber stepped down as CEO in January and left the board in February . He publicly launched his shareholder campaign on Sept. 9, after submitting his three proposals to Freightos in July. He remains a 6% shareholder in the company.
Schreiber argued that Freightos should prioritize growth of its Platform business, which facilitates digital freight bookings, rather than its Solutions segment, which sells software and data products to logistics companies. He has also questioned the company’s emphasis on software, arguing that advances in artificial intelligence could make those products easier to replicate.
The advisory resolution and proxy card dispute
Schreiber’s second proposal calls for the board to appoint a chairman with experience scaling growth-stage technology companies and refocus the company’s strategy on rapid growth, with greater emphasis on its Platform segment. The recommendation is advisory and nonbinding, meaning the board would not be required to act on it even if shareholders approve it.
Despite that, the board still defended its current strategy, arguing that its solutions and platform businesses support one another.
“The Board believes that prioritizing near-term Platform growth at the expense of this integrated approach could undermine the very foundations of the company’s long-term growth potential,” Freightos said.
The company argued that the recommendation was “abstract and imprecise” because it combined two separate issues: the qualifications of the board chairman and the company’s business strategy. Both matters, Freightos said, fall within the board’s authority rather than shareholders’ rights under the company’s articles of association. Freightos also specified how shareholders’ proxy votes would be counted on the proposal. “The shares represented by this proxy, when properly executed, will also be voted “against” PROPOSAL 4,” Freightos said.
Schreiber criticized the provision, arguing that it undermines shareholders’ ability to exercise their voting rights.
“They said something which I believe is completely, you know, essentially rigging the vote,” Schreiber said. “It’s a very basic principle of corporate law that shareholders can vote. It says it in the articles… I don’t understand it.”
The only way a shareholder will be able to vote in favor of the resolution is if they show up in-person at Freightos’ offices in Modi’in, Israel. Schreiber said he does not expect shareholders to attend in person.
“In practice, I can tell you, I was managing these meetings. Virtually zero, if not zero shareholders actually travel,” Schreiber said. “If I remember correctly, last year, there was zero people actually voting in person at the meeting.”
Freightos’ responses to Schreiber’s other proposals
The first proposal is to remove Lange from the board, a move Schreiber tied to Freightos’ growth and decline in its share price since Lange became chairman in July 2025. Freightos shares had fallen approximately 62% between July 28, 2025, and Sept. 8, 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite gained about 25%, according to Schreiber’s campaign . Using historical closing prices from Nasdaq for both dates, Freightos shares show a slightly smaller decline of approximately 59%, while confirming the Nasdaq’s roughly 25% gain. These figures reflect a different measurement period than those in FreightWaves’ earlier coverage , which found that over the preceding 12 months, Freightos shares had fallen about 78%, while the Nasdaq Composite had gained roughly 16%.
Freightos’ board argued that removing Lange before the end of his term would disrupt leadership continuity as the company works toward profitability . Lange was re-elected to the board in 2025 with 99.9% of votes cast by shareholders present at the meeting, according to the proxy statement. Schreiber also voted in favor of Lange’s re-election in 2025, but has since changed his position following disagreements over Freightos’ strategic direction.
“Removing the independent Chairman of the Board in the middle of his elected term would disrupt the continuity of the Board’s leadership and oversight at an important stage in the Company’s development,” the company said in the proxy statement.
The board also questioned the broader rationale behind Schreiber’s proposal.
“The proposal could be perceived as a mechanism targeting a specific incumbent (Lange) rather than establishing a durable, principle-based governance standard.”
The third proposal would amend Freightos’ articles of association to require annual elections for all directors beginning in 2027. Directors currently serve staggered three-year terms, with different classes standing for election at successive annual meetings.
Schreiber argued that annual elections for all directors is generally good business practice, separate from his disagreements with Freightos’ current leadership and business strategy.
Freightos opposes the change.
“This stability allows management to resist short-term market pressures and enables uninterrupted focus on achieving key financial milestones,” the company said in the filing.
Voting requirements and deadlines
The proposals carry different voting requirements. Removing Lange as chairman and approving Schreiber’s advisory recommendation each require a majority of votes cast by eligible shareholders. The proposed amendment to Freightos’ articles of association, which would establish annual elections for all directors, requires approval by at least two-thirds of votes cast.
Shareholders will also vote on Freightos’ own proposals to re-elect directors Ezra Gardner and Pablo Pinillos and reappoint EY Israel as the company’s independent auditor. The board recommended voting in favor of both proposals.
Shareholders of record as of Nov. 5 became eligible to vote. Votes must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. EST on Dec. 15 to be counted.
Why this matters
The dispute puts Freightos shareholders in the middle of a debate over the company’s leadership, governance and long-term strategy. The outcome could influence who oversees the business, how directors are elected and whether Freightos shifts its focus toward its digital freight-booking platform.

Cellectis’ business transformation could cost around 160 global employees their jobs. The company has stopped enrollment in its two CAR T programs as it focuses on trials of its in vivo candidates.
Two months after announcing it would shift away from allogeneic CAR T cell therapies to focus on in vivo therapies, Cellectis has disclosed that the move will likely trigger a global headcount reduction of up to 70%.
The biotech had 229 full-time employees as of Dec. 31, 2025, meaning the layoffs could affect as many as 160 people.
The ongoing realignment of Paris-based Cellectis’ operating model is expected to impact employees over the rest of the year and into 2027, according to a Nov. 12 announcement . The biotech did not specify how many employees would be affected at its locations in Paris, New York and Raleigh, North Carolina.
A Cellectis spokesperson declined to provide additional details about the layoffs to BioSpace , noting that the organizational realignment is subject to the French works council consultation process and applicable French and U.S. labor law requirements.
In September, Cellectis announced that its board of directors had approved a strategic transformation to become an in vivo gene editing company focused on developing treatments for chronic diseases. The decision reflects the biotech’s progress with its HEAL-101 and HEAL-201 programs and an assessment of where it could most effectively deploy its gene editing capabilities, André Choulika, co-founder and CEO, said in the announcement.
HEAL-101 is an in vivo base editing candidate that targets APOC3 for severe hypertriglyceridemia, while HEAL-201 is an in vivo epigenetic editing candidate that targets PCSK9 for severe hypercholesterolemia. Hypertriglyceridemia occurs when there are too many triglycerides in a person’s blood, increasing heart disease risk. Hypercholesterolemia involves high cholesterol levels in the blood, which can cause heart disease.
Cellectis said it plans to begin an investigator-initiated trial (IIT) of HEAL-101 in China and should deliver first clinical data in the second half of 2027. In addition, a Phase 1 IIT trial is planned for HEAL-201 in China. Preliminary clinical data for that trial are expected in the first half of 2028.
Regarding its move away from CAR T cell therapies, Cellectis has stopped enrollment in its lasme-cel and eti-cel clinical programs, and site closeout activities are in progress, according to the announcement. The company continues to monitor treated patients in accordance with protocol-specified follow-up requirements.
As of Sept. 30, Cellectis had $149 million in consolidated cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and fixed-term deposits classified as current and noncurrent financial assets. The company expects it can fund its operations into the second half of 2028.

2027 Acura Integra Type S Debuts Minor Changes, Welcomes Limited-Run Heritage Edition

Acura's most exciting model for 2027 builds on the outgoing Integra Type S in many ways. Redesigned cabin materials and new exterior finishes open the list of changes, followed by several convenience features. The Honda-controlled marque hasn't touched the 2.0-liter turbo inline-four engine or the six-speed transaxle, but Acura did make a case for a special edition that you can only have in yellow.
The 2027 model year ITS is rocking standard yellow brake calipers, accompanied by gloss-black wheels and mirror caps. Hopping inside reveals dark gray trim across the door panels, instrument panel, and shifter surround. There's also a new diamond pattern for the instrument panel, whereas gloss-black knobs for the HVAC system provide additional contrast.
Prospective customers get precisely three redesigned upholstery choices, beginning with Ebony and yellow goodies. Yellow perforations on the seats are joined by yellow stitching for the steering wheel's rim, door panels, shifter boot, and center console. Orchid upholstery includes microsuede stripes in blue, whereas the Red interior theme combines red with contrasting black microsuede.
In regard to convenience, the driver's seat now comes with memory. A memory brake hold function will also make the driver's life easier, and the same can be said about the reverse-tilt functionality for both side mirrors. Under the skin, you get a familiar FWD machine with VTEC oomph.
This year, Acura quotes 320 horsepower at 6,500 revolutions per minute and no fewer than 310 pound-feet (420 Newton-meters) from 2,600 through 4,000 revolutions per minute. Its three-pedal box is a familiar auto rev-matching unit with a limited-slip differential for good measure, so yeah, Acura didn't bother changing what was perfectly so from the outset.
Photo: Acura When it comes to pricing, $54,600 from the outset is a lot for a compact. Adding the $1,395 destination charge results in five bucks under $56,000, and that is before taxes, registration, and similar expenses. The EPA fuel consumption estimates remain unchanged: 21 mpg in the city, 28 highway, and 24 in the combined test cycle, equivalent to 9.8 l/100 km.

Marking three decades since the DC2 ITR made its American debut, the special edition brings back the spirit of Phoenix Yellow. The company is calling this hue Blazing Phoenix Yellow, and the color represents a more vibrant interpretation of the yellow offered back in the day. This paint option also marks the first time since MY01 that Acura has offered yellow on the Integra.
Black exterior badging, copper-finished alloy wheels boasting a 10-spoke design, and an exclusive titanium shift knob inspired by the JDM ITR are featured. Every Heritage Edition sports the Ebony and yellow interior. $56,900 is the advertised starting price of the most exciting Integra available for 2027, and this version carries the same EPA fuel economy ratings.
Acura intends to showcase the Integra Type S Heritage Edition at Super Street After Dark in Santa Ana, California, on November 19, followed by the LA Auto Show from November 19 through 29. As with the regular ITS, the HE will also reach dealers in December 2026.

1959 Ford Thunderbird Convertible Packs Super Rare Factory Options, One-Year Livery
62 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Name the biggest engine in regular passenger cars sold new in 1959 in America. Cadillac wasn’t the biggest gun. Imperial had a 413, which shoved the Caddy in third, at 390 cubes. Top dog that year was, believe it or not, a Ford. Made by the Ford division of Ford Motor Company. You guessed it, it was the Thunderbird. Sportscar personality, luxury car roominess and comfort. Here’s one to make you a believer.
When Ford retired the original two-seat Thunderbird after 1957 in favor of a larger four-seat personal luxury layout for 1958, purists scoffed , yet buyers flooded showrooms across America. Riding a 113-inch unibody wheelbase, the second-generation Square Bird captured the 1958 Motor Trend Car of the Year award and saw output nearly double from 37,892 units in 1958 to 67,456 cars in 1959, including 57,195 hardtops and 10,261 convertibles built overall.
While total second-generation production reached 198,191 units across three model years, finding an open-air 1959 example equipped with a manual gearbox is an exercise in extreme automotive detective work. Precisely the job for Lou Costabile, the avid classic car vlogger, who has one on his latest video. Owner John McCarthy bought his 1959 Ford Thunderbird Convertible, a factory 3-speed manual enhanced with the optional $145 Borg-Warner overdrive.
Although the 3-speed manual transmission was standard equipment on the 1959 Thunderbird, contemporary buyers overwhelmingly paid $242 extra for the Cruise-O-Matic automatic gearbox to match the car's boulevard-cruiser persona. According to McCarthy, historians estimate that only 2% of 1959 Thunderbird production left the Wixom, Michigan assembly plant with a manual transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Roughly half of those, or barely 1% of the entire model year run, received the highway-friendly overdrive unit. Now add the convertible body to the equation, and the numbers become almost a whisper compared to the total volume of personal luxury cars made that year. We can safely say “cars,” not “Fords,” because the T-bird was all alone in the field. It stayed lonely until Pontiac joined the fray in 1962, with the Grand Prix.
Out of the 67,456 examples assembled for the model year, the hardtops covered 57,195 orders, leaving 10,261 ragtops; 1,168 of those convertibles came with a 430 V8. Since we’re at it, note that 3,154 hardtops had the big motor , a $177 extra in 1959. The overdrive 3-speed manual was $145, while the Cruise-O-Matic 3-speed automatic cost a breathtaking $242. The convertible was $3,979 back then – quite a lot of money for a Ford.
Beyond its mechanical scarcity, McCarthy's convertible stands out for its elusive exterior finish, known on the 1959 Ford palette as Cordovan. From a distance, the finish mimics Raven Black, but closer inspection under direct sunlight reveals a complex, deep purple metallic base infused with chocolate brown and crimson undertones. Cordovan was a single-year color for 1959, one of 17 solid shades offered before Ford substituted a lighter maroon for 1960.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Up front, the 1959 Thunderbird replaced the 1958 model's honeycomb mesh with bold horizontal chrome bars, a design both McCarthy and Costabile regard as the handsomest grille of the second generation (1958-1960). Dual headlights sit beneath canted sheetmetal eyebrows above prominent bumper guards that the Youtuber compares to bulldog fangs.
Now I, you, and everybody else won’t be able to unsee it), while a functional hood scoop, winged Thunderbird fender-top ornaments, chrome door spears, and custom-painted rear fender skirts complete the sleek side profile.
Those rear fender skirts were missing when McCarthy acquired the car two years ago, prompting him to source a correct pair and have them painted to match. Along the flanks, the subtle tailfins originate mid-door, enveloping the arrow-shaped door handles before sweeping past the rear quarters. At the tail, 4 round lamps with three-pointed chrome bezels sit over a horizontal grille that mirrors the front fascia, predating 1960's six-taillight layout.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile A sculpted channel pressed down the center of the rear decklid visually bridges the exterior and cabin, aligning with the interior console that runs forward to the dashboard. Because the convertible uses no soft boot cover, stowing the roof involves pulling a release latch, manually lifting the rear-hinged decklid, and engaging a mechanical support lock before flipping a trunk-mounted switch that powers the hydraulic top into the plaid-lined luggage well.
Whereas the 1960 Thunderbird introduced a fully automated decklid and roof cycle, the 1959 mechanism remains semi-automatic, guided by a factory instruction sheet still affixed inside the trunk lid near the upright spare tire. Play the video and watch the owner demonstrating the roof-folding maneuver in real time.
Inside the cabin , Ford stylists enforced strict ordering rules for Cordovan cars, forbidding black or white upholstery and permitting only solid camel leather or McCarthy's two-tone tan and ivory vinyl bucket seats and matching door panels.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Behind the white steering wheel, a ribbed aluminum instrument panel houses a 140-mph speedometer showing 2,498 miles, flanked by fuel and temperature gauges, bird-shaped turn indicators, and an audible mechanical clock. Down below, a trio of pedals share space with the under-dash overdrive handle, which engages the auxiliary unit when pushed inward.
Raising the front-hinged hood reveals the standard 352-cubic-inch Thunderbird Special V8, which McCarthy removed in 2025 for a comprehensive detailing. Equipped with a four-barrel carburetor and a 10.2:1 compression ratio, the 5.8-liter powerplant produces 300 hp at 4,600 rpm and 395 lb-ft of torque at 2,800 rpm.
This brings us back to the opening question of this story. The bigger T-bird of the second generation offered a big engine for customers who felt a bit let down by the regular 352. The Blue Oval introduced the alternative – and did they overdo it! 430 cubic inches (seven liters) was a lot of engine for 1959. Lincoln and Mercury had it on their cars, of course, but Ford had the big idea: why not put it in the compact Thunderbird?
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile Remember, that was 1959 – there was “big,” and there was “bigger.” The Thunderbird was the least big car in the Ford arsenal. And it could be optioned with Detroit’s biggest engine. The optional 430-cubic-inch V8 delivered 350 hp and 490 lb-ft. But it had one major downside: it could only be paired with an automatic. Only the 352 could bring three pedals in the car, and the first owner of this T-bird, a lady from Ohio, ordered it just like that.
Dressed in factory-correct blue valve covers alongside an unusual, period-authentic white air cleaner housing and matching white four-blade cooling fan (most probably the coolest looking color scheme on any engine), the 352 V8 exhales through a single exhaust pipe.
Despite its meticulous condition, the convertible's early history remains a mystery that McCarthy hopes enthusiasts can solve. He’s been actively scouring the internet for stories about his car ever since he got it. he also tried to sell it, in March of 2025, some five months after he bought it, but the high bid on Bring a Trailer stopped at $16,250. For reference, note that in 2006, the same car also failed to find a buyer, at $33k, at a Hersey, PA, auction.

1967 Chevelle 4-Speed Is a True 138 SS 396 Time Capsule: 8,767 Miles, Knee Knocker, No One Wants It
73 photos
Photo: Mecum (2023)
When Chevrolet introduced the Chevelle for the 1964 model year, it created the most popular mid-size automobile ever built in Motor City. Across 3 generations spanning 1964 to 1977, General Motors produced approximately 4,880,000 Chevelles. To inject showroom excitement from day 1, Chevrolet launched the Super Sport trim in 1964 as the Malibu SS, selling 76,860 units equipped with inline-sixes or small-block 283-cubic-inch and 327-cubic-inch V8 engines up to 300 horsepower.
After adding the 350-horsepower 327-cubic-inch L79 V8 in 1965, Chevrolet unleashed the SS 396 mid-year under the Z16 option, building 201 cars with a 375-horsepower 396-cubic-inch V8. The SS 396 became a standalone series in 1966 with 72,272 units, followed by 63,006 in 1967 and 62,785 in 1968. Reclassified as an option package, it hit its all-time peak of 86,307 cars in 1969 before logging 53,599 units in 1970.
Before the Super Sport badge retired from the Chevelle lineup after 1973, buyers could also order 307-cubic-inch, 350-cubic-inch, and 454-cubic-inch V8 engines, capped by the 450-horsepower LS6 454 in 1970. Still, the first-generation 1967 SS 396 remains a collector favorite, which explains the buzz surrounding an Ermine White 1967 Chevelle SS 396 sport coupe recently advertised on Facebook without a listed price as a once-in-a-lifetime buy with 8,767 actual miles.
The brief social media listing touts a genuine 138-series Super Sport retaining its numbers-matching 396-cubic-inch V8, 4-speed manual transmission, factory AM/FM radio, knee-knocker tachometer, and original redline tires stored alongside the car. Bearing VIN 138177A179513, this hardtop rolled off the Atlanta, Georgia assembly line in June 1967 wearing code C-C Ermine White paint over a blue Strato-bucket seat interior.
Photo: Mecum (2023) Known on its show board as the Car From Coonbottom, the Chevelle was purchased new at Miller Chevrolet in Havana, Florida, by Willie Richardson. Living in the rural Coonbottom area outside Havana, Richardson took immense pride in his muscle car, sheltering it inside a wood-and-tin lean-to with tarps covering the open sides. For 20 years, he cranked the engine regularly, rarely drove the vehicle, and turned down every purchase offer.
When Richardson passed away in 1987, the odometer registered just 5,300 miles. His daughter inherited the coupe and promptly traded it toward a new car to David Stalling of Stalling's Motors in Cairo, Georgia. Fellow Cairo dealer Medford Stewart of Classic Auto Sales, who had chased the Chevelle for years, happened by Stalling's lot right after it arrived and immediately talked his friend into selling him the coveted low-mileage prize.
A February 1993 magazine feature also linked the 325-horsepower coupe to Quincy, Florida enthusiast Bo Deane before it spent several years in a local museum. William S. Brock of Quincy acquired the Chevelle in 1996, and its next owner bought it in November 1998 with 6,688 miles. Recently offered by Alexander Auto in Taylorsville, North Carolina, it also hit GAA Classic Cars in July 2026, stalling at a $77,000 high bid.
Photo: Mecum (2023) Having also appeared on Mecum in 2023 , eBay in December 2025, and duPont Registry before returning to GAA in November 2026, the coupe carries a December 5, 2022 certificate from Maryland appraiser Jerry MacNeish. MacNeish verified its original L35 325-horsepower 396-cubic-inch V8 engine paired with a Muncie M20 wide-ratio 4-speed transmission, and a Buffalo-cast rear axle exhibiting a factory stamping anomaly.
Despite its verified mileage and drivetrain, members of the Yenko.net Supercar Registry forum challenged early dealer descriptions calling the Chevelle an untouched time capsule. One commenter who inspected the Havana, Florida car nearly 20 years ago confirmed the mileage is authentic but lamented that the body received a full repaint instead of careful preservation. Forum experts also noted black-sprayed floors and frame rails, a re-spatter-painted trunk, and a repainted engine.
Both MacNeish and Yenko.net sleuths flagged the painted hood latch and hinges, which came in dark gray phosphate, alongside replacement hose clamps, cogged belts, and an added passenger-side mirror never available in 1967. Moreover, forum specialists observed that its U16 tachometer is a 1966 knee-knocker unit rather than a 1967 blinker tach, the U69 AM/FM radio conflicts with the leaning U73 rear antenna, and the wheels lack 6 A3 codes.
Photo: GAA Classic Cars Even with those cosmetic deviations, a low-mileage 1967 Chevelle SS 396 represents a cornerstone of Chevrolet performance. Among 403,963 Chevelles built for 1967, exactly 63,006 were domestic SS 396 models, split between 59,685 sport coupes starting at $2,825 and 3,321 convertibles priced at $3,033. Buyers could upgrade from the standard 325-horsepower L35 396 V8 to the 350-horsepower L34 for $105.35, or select the 375-horsepower solid-lifter L78 ordered on 612 cars.
On the street, the 1967 Chevelle SS 396 delivered serious muscle value, clocking a 0-to-60-mph sprint in 6.5 seconds and a 14.9-second quarter-mile run at 96.5 mph during period testing by Motor Trend. In the 1967 Detroit sales race, Chevrolet's 63,006 big-block intermediates trailed only the segment-leading Pontiac GTO, which found 81,722 buyers, while comfortably outpacing Oldsmobile's 24,829 Cutlass 4-4-2s, Ford's 20,700 Fairlane GTs, and Buick's 13,845 Skylark GS models.
Chrysler's big-block B-bodies posted smaller numbers in 1967, with Plymouth moving roughly 12,000 GTXs and Dodge building 10,809 Coronet R/Ts. This Chevy Chevelle SS 396 is hoping to break the curse that's been following it since 2023, and find a new owner, but the asking price is probably a personal matter between the seller and whoever is willing to haggle for it.

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.
The Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.
Two price hikes in a week
Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:
Dual Motor AWD: $82,490, not orderable
Premium AWD: $92,490, not orderable
Cyberbeast: $109,990, the only trim you can select
Tesla’s US Cybertruck configurator on November 13, 2026: the Dual Motor and Premium AWD are greyed out (Screenshot: Electrek)
A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
On November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor . That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.
New inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search showed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.
So much for the backlog
This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”
If there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.
But the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3 , a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”
That’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.
Some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t said whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

I have been a huge Tesla Motors fan since 2009 when they released the Model S concept, and put an early deposit on Model S. I think we are seeing the beginning of Tesla phasing out consumer vehicles. It's too bad.

This is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.
I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we said it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.
If you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper new option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

source_document.body:
CMA CGM reported a sharp increase in third-quarter earnings today as higher freight rates and growing container volumes strengthened its ocean container business.
The third-largest liner operator said weaker profitability in logistics highlighted uneven conditions across the group. Net profit reached $2.32 billion, compared with about $760 million a year earlier.
The Marseilles-based company said revenue rose 31.1% to $18.4 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization climbed 61.6% to approximately $4.8 billion. The group’s EBITDA margin widened to 25.9%, an improvement of 4.9 percentage points from the third quarter of 2025.
“In an uncertain geopolitical environment, the Group has delivered a strong performance in the third quarter, driven by the momentum and the increasing volumes of our maritime activities,” Chairman and Chief Executive Rodolphe Saade said in the earnings announcement.
CMA CGM carried 6.5 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) during the quarter, up 5.5% from a year earlier. The company said that growth outpaced the broader market and ranked among its strongest volume increases in recent years.
Shipping revenue increased 37.3% to $12.3 billion, substantially faster than cargo volumes, as average revenue per TEU rose 30% to $1,891. The division’s EBITDA reached $4 billion, compared with $2.2 billion a year earlier, while EBITDA margin expanded by 7.5 percentage points to 32.4%. That was ahead of Maersk’s (OTC: AMKBY ) 29.4 % and Hapag-Lloyd’s ( HLAG.DE ) 24.9 % .
The group attributed resilient demand to companies rebuilding inventories in the face of geopolitical uncertainty; investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers, and growth in clean technologies and electric vehicles, particularly in China.
Persistent tensions in the Middle East continued to disrupt shipping routes and global supply chains, bolstering rates. CMA CGM was one of the few global lines over the past several years that maintained some services through the Red Sea. It and other carriers have recently expanded the return of scheduled rotations through the full Suez Canal route.
Logistics growth fails to translate into stronger margins
The logistics business delivered higher sales but lower earnings. Revenue increased 19.2% to $5.46 billion, supported by organic growth and changes in the scope of the business. EBITDA, however, fell 14.4% to $366 million.
The division’s EBITDA margin narrowed to 6.7%, down 2.6 percentage points. CMA CGM cited difficult conditions in freight forwarding and persistent weakness in the automotive sector, contrasting with the stronger profitability of its maritime operations.
The CEVA Logistics unit expanded its international presence through the acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain and began simplifying its organizational structure.
CMA CGM continued investing in ships, terminals and air freight capacity, including three new 24,000-TEU LNG-powered containerships on its flagship Asia–Europe FAL service.
Demand outlook positive, but risks remain
CMA CGM said strong shipping demand was expected to continue over the coming months, with freight rates that have risen since the second quarter also supporting business growth. It nevertheless cautioned that Middle East tensions continued to disrupt routes and increase operating costs, while changing trade policies could reshape international cargo flows.
Why it matters: Higher freight rates and resilient demand are boosting shipping profits, but those forces are not necessarily translating into stronger profitability across the supply chain.

The Los Angeles improved-class attack submarine USS Hampton (SSN 767) enters Dry Dock 1 at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard March 8, 2025. (US Navy photo by Branden Bourque)
WASHINGTON — Submarine maintenance delays improved in fiscal 2026, with a more than 600-day drop in maintenance delays from previous years, according to the Pentagon’s first-ever submarine czar.
Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DPRM) for Submarines , said that while the service faced roughly 1,400 days of maintenance delay for submarines in both FY24 and FY25, that number was down to 780 in FY26.
“I want to highlight the significant reduction in days of maintenance delay,” Gaucher said Thursday at the Naval Submarine League Annual Symposium . “That’s more than 40 percent improvement.”
“And I attribute a significant part of this to investments made in Virginia-class spare parts over the past few years. … I expect maintenance delays will drop further in fiscal year ‘27 to around 500 days,” he continued.
Specifically, Gaucher pointed to the Virginia-class submarines John Warner and Illinois, which will be delivered for depot maintenance in a “few weeks.” While both are late for delivery in comparison to their original schedules, they are “several months early to their re-baseline schedules, and that’s something we were not even able to come close to doing several years ago,” according to Gaucher.
The service needed to update the delivery schedules, or “re-baseline,” on several occasions, Gaucher said. “So getting early to the re-baseline is a huge mark of progress. And as of today, every fast attack submarine in Portsmouth Naval Shipyard and Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard is on plan, with several — I dare say — tracking early to plan.”
The Navy has routinely suffered from submarine maintenance delays, and an August Government Accountability Office report determined public shipyards, which perform maintenance on nuclear-powered vessels like submarines, completed only 11 percent of submarine depot maintenance periods on schedule between FY16-25.

source_document.body:
New York–It is increasingly clear that before the end of 2026, the New York City Council will likely pass legislation that will be called the Delivery Protection Act, a law that from the start had Amazon and its Delivery Service Provider (DSP) model in its sights.
What is not known is what will be in it. But it won’t be the same as what was originally introduced.
The Act, which has the the backing of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani , was considered draconian by Amazon and its DSPs when first introduced in February. They saw in it a threat to the basic Amazon business model where an individually-owned DSP, not the e-commerce giant, delivers the actual packages and employs the workers under a contract with Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN).
In New York City, there are about 100 individually-owned DSPs under that structure.
But given the bill’s requirement that what it refers to as a “last mile facility operator” would need to be licensed by the city, and that other requirements governing what a last mile facility operator can and can not do (third party subcontracting would be banned), the law if passed as first introduced would effectively require Amazon to buy up all its NYC DSPs.
Who’s your employer?
And then the workers who are now employed by a DSP would become Amazon employees, getting their W-2 tax form from that company.
The hammer in the proposed law that could require Amazon to do a lot of things it might not want to do otherwise is the provision that “any license may be suspended or revoked by the commissioner, upon due notice and hearing, for the failure of a licensee to comply with any applicable provision of law or any rule duly promulgated by the commissioner.”
But at a rally Thursday on the steps of New York’s City Hall, in a driving rain with lightning overhead accompanied by cracks of thunder, and in separate discussions, the growing consensus is that whatever comes out of the City Council and signed by the mayor will not be the bill as it is currently written.
What happens with the legislation could have national implications.
The model of the New York Delivery Protection Act is being proposed in Chicago. Although there are not known to be any other cities where the Delivery Protection Act model is being pursued, what is happening in New York has drawn national coverage and might not be limited to New York and Chicago if it passes.
The rally, sponsored by New York Delivers, a coalition that includes Amazon, was not the first gathering on the steps of City Hall by the DPSs. There was a similar rally in April , before the only hearing that has taken place on the bill. Opponents of the bill also made their voices heard at City Hall in February.
The April rally was a dueling showdown of advocates; a large group of Delivery Protection Act backers, organized by the Teamsters, also demonstrated that day. The Teamsters also held a City Hall rally last month.
Not getting public City Council backing
One big difference between the two recent gatherings: there have been City Council members beyond bill sponsor Tiffany Caban at the Teamsters rallies. There have not been City Council members at the New York Delivers events. (Although one City Council member who had backed the bill recently switched sides , generating coverage in The New York Post.)
Business leaders make their stand
What the forces fighting the Delivery Protection Act have are all five of the city’s borough-based Chambers of Commerce, which have focused on the core argument against the Caban bill: the DSPs are locally-owned small businesses, with more than a quarter of them led by people of color. They are in all five boroughs, led by entrepreneurs, employing thousands. Some of them are veterans.
Opponents of the bill also argue there is no guarantee that if the Delivery Protection Act passes as is, the legality of the mandate for a last mile delivery company to hire workers cut loose by the company is questionable and that the enforcement mechanism of denying a re-licensing could still leave workers out of a job while the process plays out.
The other scenario raised by the bill’s opponents would be for Amazon to move some of its warehouse-based activities across borders–into Nassau County from Queens, into Westchester County from the Bronx, for example–and have the DSPs pick up their packages there.
“I think we are at a point where the City Council clearly wants to move something, and there are negotiations happening now about what the final bill is going to look like,” Jessica Walker, president and CEO of the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, told FreightWaves at the rally. Walker also addressed the crowd standing on the City Hall steps.
She added that the negotiations are not with the outside opponents on one side of the table, arguing against the bill. Rather, Walker said, “all the Council members have to talk to one another and figure out the best route.”
The role of the speaker
Another key player in the process will be Julie Menin, speaker of the City Council.
A recent article in The New York Times cited sources that said Menin “is concerned that the bill might cost the city jobs and lead Amazon to jack up prices.”
But with the bill having enough co-sponsors to pass easily, as long as the speaker allows it to get to the City Council floor, Menin also provided a statement to the Times that was broadly in support of the legislation.
Council speaker Julie Menin
“New York City regulates everything from nail salons to barbershops, yet major online retailers like Amazon have gone unregulated for far too long,” she said, according to the Times. “It’s time for Amazon to adhere to a licensing framework that ensures fair pay, strong worker protections and more responsible delivery practices that don’t leave vehicles idling on our streets for hours.”
Lawyer up!
What is accepted by all sides is that if–when–the bill passes and is signed by the mayor, lengthy litigation will commence. Given that, backers of the bill reportedly are looking for compromise legislation that would take certain issues out of any subsequent litigation and more easily get to some form of regulation.
To do that, the final bill may fall short of the nuclear option that would effectively require Amazon to purchase the DSPs.
Walker said of the negotiations going on within the Council that “what we want to do is get a solid bill that is going to address the concerns that we all have about street safety and worker protection.The problem is the bill as draft doesn’t do that.”
Some of the issues raised by the backers of the bill that seem ripe for compromise might target delivery quotas at DSPs, with the idea that drivers under mandates for delivering a large number of packages in a period of time that seems like a herculean task could also be contributing to traffic safety issues.
“Studies show the big problem is around street safety, especially around the warehouses,” Walker said. She added that there already are multiple city agencies that deal with worker safety, as well as federal involvement. “So to the extent that they are not protecting workers, then we need to ramp up their enforcement activities,” Walker said.
“We’re putting forward other solutions that we think would actually do more, while again not eliminating 100 small businesses in the five boroughs,” Walker said.
Why isn’t it good for us?
Randy Peers, the president and CEO of the Brooklyn Chamber of Commerce, addressed the City Hall rally with a fiery short speech that contained a few expletives. Peers was probably the most vociferous opponent at a panel of the Chamber of Commerce executives at the April hearing.
Citing the number 1,137, Peers said “that’s the amount of subcontractors just the (city’s Department of Transportation ) uses. Eighty five of those subcontractors are under the category of courier trucking or logistics. They spend $458 million in subcontracted work. Same model, same city, different rules. Why is that? If it’s good enough for the city and the city agencies, why is it not good enough for these workers here?”
Role of FedEx
One question being raised by the opponents of the bill is why has FedEx (NYSE: FDX) not been as obviously active in the fight, unlike Amazon.
The FedEx model is similar to how Amazon is structured, though their individual contractors are called Independent Service Providers (ISPs). They are not owned by FedEx, and for some of them, their owners could be individuals that also own one or multiple Amazon DSPs.
FedEx is a member of the New York Delivers coalition. But it’s also notable that at rallies pushing back against the bill, Amazon DSP owners are highlighted, and many of the workers attending the gatherings wear their Amazon-branded garb. FedEx is barely mentioned.
But the backers of the bill, at their rallies, barely mention FedEx either.
An email sent to FedEx had not been responded to by publication time.
